                             Object Detection

Figure 1. ZS/FSOD challenges and the traditional method. Left: Two challenges—data scarcity and catastrophic forgetting. Right:
Representative methods: (a) Traditional transfer learning pipelines requiring two-stage training and finetuning; (b) zero-shot detectors based
on VLMs, which rely on large-scale visual pre-training but adapt poorly on the FSOD benchmarks; (c) AgentDet, a multi-agent system
with a shared blackboard that aggregates evidence regarding both base and new classes at the fragment level into a unified knowledge base.

Blackboard; Agent-Judge reads the Shared Blackboard then                                      without architectural changes.

Figure 2. AgentDet overview. The query image is processed by four agents collaborating: Scout writes holistic textual cues (H), Pinner
pins fragment-level visual cues retrieved from the Knowledge Base (R), Curator performs pseudo-incremental safe updates to the KB, and
Judge reads the board to output final detections (B, ω).

tings. More importantly, most existing MLLMs focus                            reflection and memory, using natural-language feedback to

As a result, their use in ZS/FSOD remains relatively limited.                 interact through dialogue or programmatic coordination, as

Zero/Few-shot Object Detection. Conventional FSOD                             training and decentralized execution (CTDE), which allows
methods mainly build on transfer learning [24, 31], meta-                     coordination to be learned jointly while keeping inference
learning [23], and data augmentation [11]. Although these                     modular.
strategies have been widely studied, they often struggle
when only a few novel-class samples are available, espe-
cially when the gap between base and novel classes is large.

Figure 3. AgentDet pipeline details. Top-left (Agent-Scout): CLIP matches region proposals to class prompts, writing holistic tex-
tual cues H. Top-right (Agent-Pinner): DINOv2 retrieves KB patches and composes fragment-level cues R. Bottom-left (Agent-
Curator): pseudo-incremental crop–oversegmentation with Match&Filter maintains the KB. Bottom-right (Agent-Judge): an LLM
consumes (R, H) with visual tokens and outputs final detections (B, ω).

detects novel objects without any training images. When                          agents during a single inference episode.
K > 0, the task is referred to as FSOD, where only a limited                        At time step t, we represent the Board state as
number of labeled images are available for each novel class.
